title: Knowledge Check 6: Lessons 26-30
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 26-30 of the ai-power-user series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Why does building a workflow get cheaper over time once you keep a library of reusable pieces?
options: Because you memorize each workflow and can rebuild it from memory
Because each new workflow starts from proven pieces instead of a blank page
Because the tools themselves get faster the more you use them
Because repeating the same task daily builds speed through habit
questions.explanation: Compounding happens when the pieces from finished work feed back into the next effort. Reusing proven templates, contracts, and connectors means the next workflow starts from working parts instead of re-solving problems you already solved.

questions.question: You keep separate copies of your house-style instructions inside each of four workflows. What does the don't-repeat-yourself principle say to do instead?
options: Keep all four, since every workflow needs its own personal copy
Delete the instructions so the tool picks whatever tone it wants
Write a longer fifth version and add it to every workflow
Keep one authoritative copy that every workflow references
questions.explanation: Duplication rots a library because a change must be made in every copy and one will be missed. Keeping a single authoritative copy that everything references means one edit fixes the behavior everywhere.

questions.question: Which piece has earned a place in your automation library?
options: A parameterized template with open slots that more than one working workflow uses
A prompt with one client's exact name and wording baked in for a single job
A connector you configured once but never actually ran
A style rule you drafted but have not yet applied anywhere
questions.explanation: A building block must be general enough to serve more than one workflow and proven by a working run. A reusable template that several workflows use passes both tests, while a single-job prompt and untested pieces fail them.

questions.question: Which selection test rules out a one-prompt job on one side and a board-level forecast project on the other?
options: It is real: you already run the task at least monthly
It is medium: three to six connected steps with real input and output contracts and a review gate
It is same-shaped: the same inputs, steps, and output every time
It is worth the build: the setup pays back on a real schedule
questions.explanation: The medium test sets a size band. A one-prompt job has too few steps to exercise the pattern, and a project that needs several systems and senior judgment is too big to finish, so both land outside the band.

questions.question: What is a definition of done for a workflow?
options: The list of tools and connectors the workflow uses
The schedule that decides when each run starts
The list of tasks you have decided are out of scope
The checklist a completed run must pass before you trust its output
questions.explanation: A definition of done is the set of checks that mark work as genuinely finished rather than finished enough to stop. For a workflow, it is the list a run must satisfy before its output is trusted.

questions.question: Which part of a scope exists specifically to stop a project from growing while you build it?
options: The one-sentence job, which names what the workflow does
The trigger, which names exactly what starts a run
The boundaries, which state what is explicitly out of scope
The inputs, which describe the exact form the data arrives in
questions.explanation: Boundaries are the section that writes down what the workflow will not do. Stating the limits on paper is what lets you honor them when someone asks for one more thing and keeps the build from drifting wider.

questions.question: When designing a pipeline, what is the cheapest way to catch a mismatch between two steps before you wire anything?
options: Run all the steps together and see which one breaks first
Add error handling to every step before the first run
Write out each step's input, action, and output in order and compare the seam between them
Wire in the schedule so real runs surface the problem
questions.explanation: One step's output is the next step's input, so writing them down together exposes a seam where the shapes do not line up. Catching that on paper costs minutes, while catching it in a broken run costs far more.

questions.question: What makes assembling a workflow from library pieces faster and more reliable than writing it from scratch?
options: Each reused piece has already been tested, so you wire known parts instead of debugging new ones
Assembly lets you skip the dry run because the whole workflow is newer
Reused pieces never fail, so the workflow needs no error handling
Assembly removes the need to define how steps pass data between them
questions.explanation: Every piece you reuse is a piece you have already proven, so the build becomes mapping data into known slots rather than re-authoring and re-testing fresh parts. Reuse is what makes assembly both faster and safer.

questions.question: What is the deliverable of the build stage, before any hardening or scheduling?
options: A workflow wired into a calendar trigger and running on its own
A pipeline that carries a real job from trigger to output and passes a dry run against your definition of done
A fully hardened workflow with retries, alarms, and every edge case covered
A polished output produced without a single dry run
questions.explanation: The build stage exists to get one complete path moving, proven against a fake or past input. Hardening and scheduling come later, because you cannot strengthen or automate a workflow that has never produced a passing run.

questions.question: What turns a review habit into a true gate?
options: Adding a second person to look at the draft as well
Sending a reminder on the morning the output is due
Moving the review earlier so there is more time to fix problems
Naming the checks, blocking delivery when one fails, recording the decision, and setting a due time
questions.explanation: A gate is built into the workflow rather than bolted on. It names the specific checks, stops delivery when one fails, records the decision, and has an owner and a deadline, so a bad output cannot proceed.

questions.question: What is a regression set used for in a hardened workflow?
options: Listing every step so a new operator can run the workflow from the page
Re-running past inputs alongside their approved outputs to confirm a change did not break anything
Recording which vendors are allowed to appear in the output
Storing every error message the workflow has produced so far
questions.explanation: A regression is when something that used to work stops working. Pairing past inputs with the outputs you approved lets you re-run them after any change and learn in minutes whether the change broke a case that used to pass.

questions.question: A run reports success but its output is quietly wrong. Which post-run check catches this class of failure?
options: Reconciling a count in the output against the count in the source and failing the run when they disagree
Raising the retry cap so a failing step gets more attempts
Writing a more detailed prompt so the draft step makes fewer mistakes
Running the first cycles in parallel with the manual process
questions.explanation: A silent failure surfaces no error, so only a check that inspects the output afterward can catch it. Count reconciliation, field presence, and expected-content checks turn a quiet failure into a loud one.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a handover test?
options: Give the runbook entry to someone who has never run the workflow and watch where they stop, since each stop is a missing field
Confirm the workflow's runtime fits within an allowed time budget
Prove the workflow's output is identical to the manual version
Check that the trigger still fires on the correct business day
questions.explanation: A document nobody has tried to follow is a document with unknown errors in it. Watching a fresh reader stop reveals the exact fields the entry is missing, turning guesses about clarity into concrete fixes.

questions.question: Which element makes a decision record genuinely useful to a future reader?
options: A detailed narrative of every option you considered and rejected
A manager's signature confirming the choice was authorized
The condition under which you would reverse the decision
A screenshot of the settings so they can be reproduced
questions.explanation: The value of a record sits in its reversal condition. A decision with no stated condition for changing it can only be argued about, while one that says what would change your mind can be revisited honestly.

questions.question: Why report a workflow's break-even in months rather than simply saying it saves time?
options: Because break-even is only meaningful after a full year of runs
Because dividing build cost by the monthly return gives a claim anyone can check, while saving time is not one
Because the monthly return should always be rounded up before dividing
Because break-even hides how much the manual task used to cost
questions.explanation: Break-even turns a vague benefit into an arithmetic one: build cost divided by the monthly saving gives the number of months to earn back the effort. That is a defensible statement, unlike an unmeasurable claim that a workflow saves time.
